Skyrizi, an interleukin inhibitor approved for psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, posted brisk sales growth that reflected both deepening market penetration in existing indications and the expanding use of the therapy in newly approved settings. title: These 3 Dividend Stocks Have Crushed the Market This Year. Here’s Why They Are Still Buys - The Globe and Mail
content: AbbVie, Gilead, and Becton, Dickinson have all beaten the S&P 500 this year. Two are Dividend Kings, and Gilead has raised its payout by 74.5% over the past decade. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks continue dominating headlines on Wall Street. That probably won't change anytime soon. But investors shouldn't be so distracted by the AI revolution that they forget there are attractive investment opportunities elsewhere. Consider the following three healthcare dividend stocks: AbbVie(NYSE:ABBV), Gilead Sciences(NASDAQ:GILD), and Becton, Dickinson(NYSE:BDX). All three have crushed broader equities this year, and they still have plenty of upside ahead for investors willing to stay the course. Read on to find out more. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » AbbVie did not perform well in the first four months of the year, but it has recovered, and its shares are now up 29% to date, while the S&P 500 has gained 10%. There are several reasons behind the drugmaker's strong performance, perhaps none more important than its two biggest growth drivers, Skyrizi and Rinvoq. These two immunology medicines are performing better than management -- and Wall Street -- expected. Considering they won't lose patent protection anytime soon, and AbbVie will face no other major loss of patent exclusivity through the end of this decade, we can expect consistent revenue and earnings growth over the medium term. Still, Skyrizi and Rinvoq will eventually face patent cliffs, with the former perhaps starting around 2033. The good news is AbbVie is preparing for that. AbbVie has strengthened its immunology pipeline through an acquisition and is looking to enter the fast-growing weight-loss market. Further, legacy products, especially its Botox franchise, should perform well over the long term. AbbVie's excellent underlying business will help support its dividend program. The company is a Dividend King, one of the corporations that have increased their payouts for at least 50 consecutive years. It would take something catastrophic for AbbVie to suspend or decrease its dividends. Until then, expect regular dividend increases alongside solid returns from the company. Gilead Sciences' shares have gained 37% this year on the back of improving financial results and solid clinical and regulatory progress. The biotech leader still makes most of its money from its HIV franchise, with medicines like Biktarvy doing much of the heavy lifting. And even though Veklury, a coronavirus medicine, is harming top-line growth, the company has performed well. Gilead Sciences' third-quarter product sales grew 13% year over year -- its fastest growth rate in this category in over a decade -- to $8.29 billion. Total revenue was $8.30 billion, up almost 7% compared to the year-ago period. Product sales excluding Veklury jumped 16% year over year. So, as Veklury continues to fade into insignificance, Gilead should record stronger top-line growth, especially as it has strengthened its HIV and oncology businesses this year with new approvals and important label expansions. The biotech giant's outlook appears stronger than it has been in a while, and its dividend program remains attractive. Gilead Sciences offers a forward yield of 2%, and it has increased its payouts by 74.5% over the past 10 years. Becton, Dickinson, a medical technology company, is finally bouncing back after several challenging years. Shares are up 43% to date. One reason for the company's strong performance is its excellent financial results. content: @mezuna from dzul kifli's Images via Canva, @Casper1774Studio from Getty Images via Canva A fund most investors have never heard of just disclosed three moves worth a look. Mizuho Markets Cayman LP’s 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 9, shows new stakes in Target (TGT) and AbbVie (ABBV), and a much bigger one in Synopsys (SNPS). The filing lists $2.12 billion of US stocks across 79 positions. (A 13F shows only what a fund held on the last day of the quarter, so it can’t tell us what it paid or why.) Target was new in the quarter, and it went straight in as the fund’s No. 5 position: 1.29 million shares worth $202 million at Sept. 30, or 9.6% of its 13F stocks. That’s far bigger than the AbbVie and Synopsys stakes combined. The turnaround under CEO Michael Fiddelke, who took over on Feb. 1, is showing up in the numbers. Comparable sales rose 5.6% in the quarter ended May 2, Target’s biggest gain since early 2022, then 3.8% in the second quarter, when it raised its full-year outlook with help from tariff refunds. Fiddelke isn’t celebrating yet: “Two strong quarters is not the goal,” he told reporters in August. Wall Street has followed the stock up, lifting its average target from $101 a year ago to $166: The stock went from $90.62 to $161.45 over the same year, so it now sits just 3% below that average, at about 17x forward earnings. The stock is up 3% since Sept. 30, and Target’s third-quarter report this week has to keep comparable sales growing to push those targets higher. TIKR tracks 38 analysts on Target. The stock is up 13% since then, and the business gave it good reason. On Oct. 30, AbbVie beat its own third-quarter guidance, with revenue up 10.3% to $17.4 billion and adjusted EPS of $3.82. Skyrizi sold $5.78 billion, up 22.7%, and Rinvoq rose 23.9%. Management raised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $13.95-$13.99 and raised the quarterly dividend 5.2% to $1.82 a share. Analysts have raised their sights all year, with the average target up from $242 to $312: That average now sits just 6% above the stock. And at about 19x forward earnings, AbbVie trades well above its five-year average of 14x and its previous quarter-end high of 18x, from September 2025. Investors are already paying for Skyrizi and Rinvoq to keep growing this fast, though management says Skyrizi’s data protection runs only to 2031. AbbVie’s 2027 guidance, due with its fourth-quarter results in early February, will show whether that price holds up. Synopsys is the smallest of the three, at 61,730 shares worth $27 million, or 1.3% of the fund. But it’s the one the fund added to, raising its share count 85% on the quarter before. The stock is up 5% since Sept. 30, yet still 16% below its 52-week high, even as the business keeps beating estimates. In early September, Synopsys reported fiscal third-quarter adjusted EPS of $3.91, against the $3.67 analysts expected, and revenue up 42.4% to $2.48 billion with Ansys, the simulation software maker it bought last year, in the numbers. It raised its full-year outlook, and the stock fell anyway. Analysts haven’t backed off. Their average target has edged up from $556 a year ago to $590: That’s 30% above the stock, which closed at $455.20, and even the lowest target, $475, sits above it. At about 26x forward earnings, Synopsys costs more than the other two, but it’s also the one where the Street sees real room to run. Target’s turnaround is real, and AbbVie’s quarter was excellent. But both stocks have already climbed to within a few percent of where Wall Street thinks they’re headed. If I could only buy one of the three right now, it’d be Synopsys. It’s the only one of the three where the business has outrun the stock. The risk is that the gap has been there all year: the average target sat at $556 a year ago, when the stock was at $393.93, and the stock has yet to close it. Synopsys also assumes no further changes to US export controls in its outlook, so trade policy could hit it. Its next report, in early December, is the next test, and the fund’s next 13F, due in mid-February, will show whether it kept adding. Since becoming an independent company, AbbVie has grown its dividend substantially, and its history of increases extends back to its time as part of Abbott Laboratories. Skyrizi and Rinvoq are AbbVie's largest growth drivers. Both medicines treat immune-related conditions such as psoriasis, arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. Each grew at a strong double-digit pace during the quarter. Humira was once the world's top revenue-generating medicine, but its sales have declined sharply since lower-cost biosimilar versions entered the market. Skyrizi and Rinvoq have more than made up for that loss, allowing AbbVie to return to strong growth. AbbVie recently presented new data showing disease control for patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Skyrizi also gained an additional approval option for Crohn's disease, and a combination therapy showed encouraging early results. The neuroscience portfolio grew strongly, led by Vraylar, Botox Therapeutic for migraines and other conditions, and the migraine treatment Ubrelvy. Oncology revenue was broadly flat, while the aesthetics portfolio, which includes Botox Cosmetic and Juvederm, declined slightly as consumer spending on cosmetic procedures stayed soft.
